script.opening: "I had that glucose drink test and they’ve told me I’ve got diabetes in pregnancy. I’m really frightened — does this mean my baby’s in danger? Have I done something wrong? I don’t really understand what it means or what happens now."

facts.text: A midwife rang 2 days ago: "the test was high and someone from the diabetes clinic will be in touch". No appointment yet. Has been reading online and scaring herself.
First baby, 27 weeks. Everything normal so far; 20-week scan fine. Baby moving well. No bleeding, no headaches, no swelling, no tummy pain. Blood pressure "fine at the last midwife check".
Bit more thirsty, but "it’s been hot". Otherwise feels well. No urine infections.
BMI 32 before pregnancy. No medicines except pregnancy vitamins (folic acid and vitamin D). No allergies. Never had a sugar test before.
Mum and two aunts have type 2 diabetes; mum is on insulin and has had "problems with her feet". Husband, Imran, is supportive. Lives with husband and his parents.
Works as a pharmacy dispenser. Mother-in-law does most of the cooking — "lots of rice and chapatis". Walks to work (15 minutes). Doesn’t smoke or drink.

Anxious and close to tears at first; you keep asking "is my baby in danger?" and "is it my fault?". Settle noticeably if the doctor explains clearly and kindly that it is common, not your fault, and that good control lowers the risks. Ask practical questions: "Will I need a caesarean?" "Will it go away afterwards?" Feel worse if given a list of scary risks without reassurance.

ice.ideas: "I think it’s because I’m overweight. I’ve caused this."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — fear and guilt: "I keep thinking the baby will be born ill, or something will go wrong at the birth." Watching her mum’s diabetes makes her fear she’ll end up the same. Worried about telling her mother-in-law what she can and can’t eat.
ice.expectations: "To know if the baby is OK, and what happens now." Expects the GP to explain; doesn’t know about the specialist clinic.

cues: "Have I done something wrong?" — guilt to address directly.
"I started reading online" — worries picked up from the internet to explore.
"My mum’s on insulin" — fear of her own future and family history of type 2 diabetes.

checkpoints.text: Explains GESTATIONAL DIABETES clearly (pregnancy-hormone-driven glucose rise, usually resolving after birth) and reduces self-blame, acknowledging her fear

Gives HONEST risk information — macrosomia/shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycaemia, polyhydramnios, pre-eclampsia, increased intervention/Caesarean, longer-term type 2 risk — balanced with the reassurance that GOOD GLUCOSE CONTROL substantially reduces these risks

Outlines MANAGEMENT — referral to the JOINT antenatal/diabetes team (within 1 week, NICE NG3), blood glucose self-monitoring/targets (fasting below 5.3; 1-hour below 7.8 or 2-hour below 6.4 mmol/L), diet and activity first-line, then metformin if targets are unmet after 1–2 weeks and/or insulin (immediately if fasting glucose is 7.0 mmol/L or more) — reassuring these are safe in pregnancy

Explains increased FETAL MONITORING (growth scans every 4 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks) and that DELIVERY is planned by the team (timing/place by control and fetal size; uncomplicated GDM no later than 40+6 weeks)

Covers POSTNATAL care and FUTURE implications — glucose usually normalises but needs a postnatal check (fasting plasma glucose at 6–13 weeks; HbA1c only after 13 weeks if fasting is not possible — NICE NG3), lifelong increased type 2 risk (annual HbA1c, NICE QS109; lifestyle), likely recurrence in future pregnancies, and encouraging breastfeeding
Addresses the "is my baby in danger?" fear and self-blame directly — honest but not catastrophising — anchoring repeatedly on the reassuring, controllable message
Checks understanding, paces the information, and ensures she leaves with a concrete next step and feeling supported rather than terrified

Safety-nets and follows up: the joint-clinic referral and monitoring plan, when to seek help (reduced fetal movements, pre-eclampsia symptoms), the postnatal glucose check and lifelong screening, and review — honest risk + reassurance + a clear plan

worked.txt: "First — you haven’t done anything wrong. Pregnancy hormones make blood sugar harder to control, and some women, especially with certain risk factors, develop this. It’s called gestational diabetes, and the good news is it usually goes away after the baby’s born."

"Is your baby in danger? Here’s the honest answer: if the sugar stays high it can make the baby grow large and cause some delivery and newborn problems. BUT — and this is the key bit — keeping your sugar well controlled hugely reduces those risks. So this is very manageable, and managing it protects your baby."

"Here’s what happens now: I’ll refer you to the joint pregnancy-and-diabetes team, who should see you within a week. You’ll check your blood sugars against targets, and we start with diet and activity — with a dietitian. If your sugars aren’t on target within a week or two, we add tablets (metformin) or insulin, which are safe in pregnancy."

"You’ll have extra scans every 4 weeks from 28 weeks to watch the baby’s growth, and the team will plan your delivery — timing and place, usually by 40 weeks and 6 days at the latest — based on your sugars and the baby’s size. It’s all individualised; you won’t be left guessing."

"After birth, your sugar usually returns to normal, but we’ll do a fasting blood sugar test between 6 and 13 weeks later. It does mean a higher chance of type 2 diabetes in future, so we’ll do a yearly HbA1c blood test and support healthy changes — and it can come back in future pregnancies, so we’d test earlier next time. Breastfeeding’s encouraged and helps."

"I know it’s a lot and frightening, but you’re in good hands and there’s a clear plan. Contact the maternity team urgently if the baby’s movements reduce, or you get bad headaches, vision changes or swelling. Let’s get that referral going and review together."

f.learning: GESTATIONAL DIABETES (GDM) is glucose intolerance arising in pregnancy (pregnancy hormones impairing glucose control), usually resolving after birth, with risk factors of raised BMI, family history, ethnicity and a previous large baby — so explain it simply and remove self-blame while acknowledging the mother’s fear. Give honest risk information balanced with reassurance: poorly controlled GDM raises the risk of a large baby (MACROSOMIA) and birth complications (shoulder dystocia), neonatal hypoglycaemia, polyhydramnios, pre-eclampsia and increased intervention/Caesarean, with longer-term type 2 diabetes risk for mother and child — but GOOD GLUCOSE CONTROL substantially REDUCES these risks, so the anchoring message is "manageable, and controlling it protects your baby", not catastrophe. Management: referral to the JOINT antenatal/diabetes (maternal medicine) team within 1 week (NICE NG3), blood glucose self-monitoring against targets (fasting below 5.3 mmol/L; 1 hour after meals below 7.8 or 2 hours below 6.4 mmol/L), diet and physical activity first-line (dietitian input), and metformin if targets are not met within 1–2 weeks, then insulin (immediate insulin if fasting glucose is 7.0 mmol/L or more at diagnosis) — metformin and/or insulin if targets are not met (reassuring these are safe in pregnancy). Explain increased fetal monitoring (growth and amniotic fluid scans every 4 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks for macrosomia/polyhydramnios) and that delivery is planned by the team (timing and place per glycaemic control and fetal size, usually avoiding prolonged pregnancy — no later than 40+6 weeks if uncomplicated). Postnatally, glucose usually normalises but needs a postnatal check (fasting plasma glucose at 6–13 weeks; HbA1c only after 13 weeks if a fasting test is not possible), with lifelong increased type 2 diabetes risk (annual HbA1c, NICE QS109; lifestyle), likely recurrence in future pregnancies (early self-monitoring or OGTT next time), higher long-term metabolic risk for the child, and breastfeeding encouraged. The communication core (and hidden agenda) is fear for the baby and self-blame; give accurate risk information WITHOUT catastrophising, repeatedly anchor on the reassuring controllable message, remove blame, check understanding, and provide a concrete next step so she leaves informed and supported.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG3 (diabetes in pregnancy, 2015, updated 2020) · [2] NICE QS109 (diabetes in pregnancy) · [3] NICE NG133 (hypertension in pregnancy, 2019)
knowledge.summary: Gestational diabetes raises risks for mother and baby, but good glucose control reduces them. Refer to the joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within a week, start monitoring, diet and activity, add metformin or insulin if targets are not met, and plan postnatal testing and lifelong screening.

points.t: NICE NG3 [1]: gestational diabetes if fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or more, or 2-hour plasma glucose is 7.8 mmol/L or more on a 75 g OGTT. Risk factors include BMI above 30, a first-degree relative with diabetes, a previous macrosomic baby, previous gestational diabetes, and family origin with a high prevalence of diabetes. Check HbA1c at diagnosis to identify pre-existing type 2 diabetes.

Higher risks of a large-for-gestational-age baby, shoulder dystocia and birth trauma, induction and caesarean birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, polyhydramnios and pre-eclampsia, with a higher later risk of type 2 diabetes for the mother. Good control reduces these risks; that is the anchor message.

NICE NG3 [1]: joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week of diagnosis. Self-monitoring targets: fasting below 5.3 mmol/L, and 1 hour after meals below 7.8 or 2 hours after meals below 6.4 mmol/L; keep above 4 mmol/L if on insulin or glibenclamide.

NICE NG3 [1]: if fasting glucose is below 7.0 at diagnosis, offer diet and exercise; add metformin if targets are not met within 1–2 weeks; add insulin if still not met, or if metformin is contraindicated or unacceptable. If fasting glucose is 7.0 or more at diagnosis, offer immediate insulin with or without metformin; consider it at 6.0–6.9 with macrosomia or hydramnios. Glibenclamide only if metformin fails and insulin is declined, or metformin is not tolerated. Doses per BNF.

NICE NG3 [1]: ultrasound of fetal growth and amniotic fluid every 4 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks. Advise women with uncomplicated gestational diabetes to give birth no later than 40+6 weeks, offering elective birth if not delivered by then; earlier if there are maternal or fetal complications.

NICE NG3 [1]: stop glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth and check glucose before transfer to community care. Fasting plasma glucose at 6–13 weeks after birth (after 13 weeks: fasting glucose, or HbA1c if a fasting test is not possible). FPG below 6.0 means low probability of diabetes; HbA1c 39–47 means high risk. Annual HbA1c thereafter if the test is negative (QS109 [2]).
NICE NG3 [1]: offer early self-monitoring of blood glucose, or an OGTT as soon as possible after booking with a further OGTT at 24–28 weeks if the first is normal.

Urgent maternity assessment for reduced fetal movements, and for pre-eclampsia symptoms: severe headache, visual disturbance, severe pain below the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet (NICE NG133 [3]).

model.text: Hello Mrs Rahman, I’m Dr Evans. Can you hear me clearly, and is now a good time to talk? … What would you like to talk about today?

I had that glucose drink test and they’ve told me I’ve got diabetes in pregnancy. I’m really frightened. Does this mean my baby’s in danger? Have I done something wrong? I don’t really understand what it means or what happens now.
I can hear how worried you are, and I’m glad you called. I’ll answer all three of those questions, starting with whether your baby is in danger. Can I first check a few things?
model.why: Acknowledges fear; commits to answering her questions

model.text: Yes, okay.
What have you been told so far, and by whom?
Just a phone call saying the test was high and someone would be in touch. Then I started reading online.
How are you feeling in yourself? Is the baby moving as normal for you?
model.why: Checks current wellbeing and fetal movements

model.text: I feel fine. Yes, the baby’s moving as usual.
Any headaches, problems with your vision, or swelling in your face or hands?
No, nothing like that.
And are you very thirsty or passing lots of urine?
No, not really.
You asked whether you’d done something wrong. What’s made you think that?
My weight, I suppose. And diabetes runs in my family. I keep thinking I’ve caused this.
Thank you for telling me. What’s your biggest fear about the baby?
That something will go wrong at the birth, or the baby will be born ill.

First, you haven’t done anything wrong. During pregnancy the placenta makes hormones that make it harder for your body to control sugar. Some women, especially with a family history, can’t keep up, so the sugar rises. That’s gestational diabetes. Weight and family history make it more likely, but it isn’t something you caused, and it usually goes away after the birth.
model.why: Explains the mechanism and removes blame

model.text: So it’s not my fault?

No. Now your main question. If the sugar stays high, the baby can grow larger than usual, which can make the birth harder, and the baby may need sugar checks after birth. There’s also a higher chance of high blood pressure in pregnancy. But keeping your sugar in the target range greatly reduces those risks. So your baby is not in danger now, and what we do next protects the baby.
model.why: Honest risks balanced with the controllable message

model.text: That’s a relief. What do I actually do?

You’ll be seen in a joint clinic with a diabetes team and the maternity team, ideally within a week. They’ll teach you to check your sugar with a finger-prick, before breakfast and after meals, against targets. You’ll see a dietitian, and a walk after meals helps a lot.
model.why: NG3 joint clinic within a week, monitoring, diet and activity

model.text: And if that doesn’t work?

If the numbers aren’t on target within a week or two, the next step is a tablet called metformin, and some women need insulin. Both are used widely in pregnancy. Needing them isn’t failing; it just means the pregnancy hormones are strong.
model.why: NG3 escalation; reassures about safety; reframes treatment

model.text: Will I need a caesarean?

Not necessarily. You’ll have extra scans to check the baby’s growth and the fluid around the baby, every four weeks from 28 weeks. The team will talk with you about when and how to have the baby, and if all is going well that’s by 40 weeks and 6 days at the latest, earlier if needed. Many women with gestational diabetes have a vaginal birth.
model.why: NG3 scans every 4 weeks from 28 to 36; birth planning

model.text: And afterwards?

Usually the sugar goes back to normal straight after birth. We’ll do a fasting blood test here between 6 and 13 weeks after the birth. Because this raises your chance of type 2 diabetes later, we’ll check a blood test every year. If you have another pregnancy, we’d test you early.
model.why: NG3 postnatal FPG, annual HbA1c, early testing next pregnancy

model.text: Contact the maternity unit straight away if the baby’s movements slow down or change, or if you get a bad headache, problems with your vision, pain under your ribs, vomiting or sudden swelling. Can you tell me in your own words what happens now?
model.why: Specific safety-net: reduced movements, pre-eclampsia symptoms; teach-back

model.text: It’s not my fault. Control the sugar and the risks go down. Joint clinic this week, finger-pricks, dietitian, maybe metformin. Scans. Blood test after the birth and every year.
Exactly right. I’ll make sure the clinic referral has gone, and let’s speak again after your first appointment.
Thank you. I feel like I can breathe again.

social.t: Weight and diabetes carry stigma; pregnant women often blame themselves. Address it directly and without judgement.
Frequent finger-prick testing, clinic visits and diet change add to pregnancy demands. Ask what support she has, without assuming.

legal.t: Pregnant women and those who have had a baby in the previous 12 months are entitled to free NHS prescriptions with a valid maternity exemption certificate.
Employees are entitled to reasonable paid time off for antenatal appointments, including the joint clinic.

professional.t: The GP’s role is to confirm the joint-clinic referral, support understanding, and record gestational diabetes so the postnatal test and annual HbA1c recall happen.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share risk information in a way the patient can understand, balanced and without undue alarm.

community.t: Record the diagnosis for recall; the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme can support women at high risk of type 2 diabetes if eligible.

redFlags: Severe headache, visual disturbance, pain below the ribs, vomiting or sudden swelling (pre-eclampsia)
Marked thirst, polyuria or feeling unwell (significant hyperglycaemia)
Fasting glucose 7.0 or more at diagnosis (immediate insulin)
psychosocial: Self-blame about weight and family history
Fear for the baby and the birth
ice: Idea: her baby is in danger and she caused it
Concern: something going wrong at birth or the baby born ill
Expectation: to understand the result and what happens next

playbook.diagnosis: “The test shows gestational diabetes: pregnancy hormones are making it harder for your body to control sugar. It usually goes away after the birth.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The placenta makes hormones that act like a brake on insulin. In most women the body presses harder on the accelerator to keep up. In some, it can’t quite, so sugar rises. We help it keep up.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if your baby is in danger and whether you caused this. You didn’t cause it, and keeping your sugar on target is exactly what protects your baby.”
management.psychosocial: Remove blame; slow the information down; follow-up call after the first clinic; signpost reliable information instead of online searching.
sharedPlan: Joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week (NG3)
Self-monitoring: fasting below 5.3; 1 hour below 7.8 or 2 hours below 6.4 mmol/L
Diet with dietitian support and activity, such as walking after meals
Metformin if targets not met in 1–2 weeks; insulin if still not met
Growth and fluid scans every 4 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks; birth planning, by 40+6 if uncomplicated
Fasting plasma glucose 6–13 weeks after birth; annual HbA1c; early testing next pregnancy
safetyNet: Maternity unit immediately for reduced or changed fetal movements
Maternity unit urgently for headache, visual change, pain below the ribs, vomiting or sudden swelling
Follow-up call after the first joint clinic

pitfalls.intro: The trap is either frightening her with a list of complications or falsely reassuring her. The marks sit in honest risk anchored on control, removing blame, and a concrete plan she can repeat.

items.fail: Listing complications with no reassuring message.
items.why: She leaves more frightened and less able to engage.
items.fix: Name the main risks, then: “Keeping your sugar on target greatly reduces them.”

items.fail: No mention of the joint clinic or its timing.
items.why: NG3 asks for review in a joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week.
items.fix: Confirm the referral and the timescale.

items.why: The postnatal fasting glucose at 6–13 weeks and annual HbA1c are commonly missed.
items.fix: “A fasting blood test 6 to 13 weeks after the birth, then every year.”

items.fail: Answering the medical questions but ignoring “Have I done something wrong?”
items.fix: “You haven’t done anything wrong. Pregnancy hormones cause this.”

items.why: Adds guilt and may reduce acceptance later.
items.fix: “Needing metformin or insulin just means the hormones are strong.”

items.fail: No safety-net for fetal movements or pre-eclampsia.
items.fix: Name reduced movements and pre-eclampsia symptoms, and who to call.

What she has been told, fetal movements, pre-eclampsia symptoms, thirst and polyuria.
Self-blame about weight and family history; fear about the birth.
Hormone mechanism, not her fault; risks named plainly, anchored on control reducing them.
Joint clinic within a week, targets, diet, metformin or insulin, scans, birth timing, postnatal test, annual HbA1c. Safety-net and teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Lists complications without reassurance, or says “it’s nothing to worry about”; no joint-clinic referral; never addresses self-blame; no postnatal or lifelong screening plan; no safety-net for fetal movements.
wordPics.pass: Explains gestational diabetes, names the main risks with the message that control reduces them, outlines joint clinic, monitoring, diet and escalation, and mentions the postnatal test.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explores and removes self-blame explicitly; answers each of her three questions in order; gives NG3 specifics (1-week clinic, 4-weekly scans, 6–13-week fasting glucose, annual HbA1c); reframes insulin as not failure; screens pre-eclampsia and movements; teach-back shows she can repeat the plan.

avoid.instead: “Pregnancy hormones cause this. Weight and family history make it more likely, but it isn’t something you did.”
avoid.why: Blame increases distress and harms engagement.

avoid.dont: “There’s a risk of stillbirth, shoulder dystocia, pre-eclampsia …”
avoid.instead: “If sugars stay high, the baby can grow larger. Keeping them on target greatly reduces that.”
avoid.why: A list of complications without the control message terrifies without helping.

avoid.dont: “If diet fails you’ll have to go on insulin.”
avoid.instead: “Some women need metformin or insulin because the hormones are strong. It isn’t failing.”
avoid.why: Framing treatment as failure adds guilt.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG3 (diabetes in pregnancy, 2015, updated 2020) · [2] NICE QS109 (diabetes in pregnancy) · [3] NICE NG133 (hypertension in pregnancy, 2019)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Gestational diabetes raises risks for mother and baby, but good glucose control reduces them. Refer to the joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within a week, start monitoring, diet and activity, add metformin or insulin if targets are not met, and plan postnatal testing and lifelong screening.

points.t: NICE NG3 [1]: gestational diabetes if fasting plasma glucose is 5.6 mmol/L or more, or 2-hour plasma glucose is 7.8 mmol/L or more on a 75 g OGTT. Risk factors include BMI above 30, a first-degree relative with diabetes, a previous macrosomic baby, previous gestational diabetes, and family origin with a high prevalence of diabetes. Check HbA1c at diagnosis to identify pre-existing type 2 diabetes.

Higher risks of a large-for-gestational-age baby, shoulder dystocia and birth trauma, induction and caesarean birth, neonatal hypoglycaemia, polyhydramnios and pre-eclampsia, with a higher later risk of type 2 diabetes for the mother. Good control reduces these risks; that is the anchor message.

NICE NG3 [1]: joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week of diagnosis. Self-monitoring targets: fasting below 5.3 mmol/L, and 1 hour after meals below 7.8 or 2 hours after meals below 6.4 mmol/L; keep above 4 mmol/L if on insulin or glibenclamide.

NICE NG3 [1]: if fasting glucose is below 7.0 at diagnosis, offer diet and exercise; add metformin if targets are not met within 1–2 weeks; add insulin if still not met, or if metformin is contraindicated or unacceptable. If fasting glucose is 7.0 or more at diagnosis, offer immediate insulin with or without metformin; consider it at 6.0–6.9 with macrosomia or hydramnios. Glibenclamide only if metformin fails and insulin is declined, or metformin is not tolerated. Doses per BNF.

NICE NG3 [1]: ultrasound of fetal growth and amniotic fluid every 4 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks. Advise women with uncomplicated gestational diabetes to give birth no later than 40+6 weeks, offering elective birth if not delivered by then; earlier if there are maternal or fetal complications.

NICE NG3 [1]: stop glucose-lowering treatment immediately after birth and check glucose before transfer to community care. Fasting plasma glucose at 6–13 weeks after birth (after 13 weeks: fasting glucose, or HbA1c if a fasting test is not possible). FPG below 6.0 means low probability of diabetes; HbA1c 39–47 means high risk. Annual HbA1c thereafter if the test is negative (QS109 [2]).
NICE NG3 [1]: offer early self-monitoring of blood glucose, or an OGTT as soon as possible after booking with a further OGTT at 24–28 weeks if the first is normal.

Urgent maternity assessment for reduced fetal movements, and for pre-eclampsia symptoms: severe headache, visual disturbance, severe pain below the ribs, vomiting, or sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet (NICE NG133 [3]).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; let her voice all three fears before explaining.
Self-blame about weight and family history explored; emotional impact acknowledged.
Picked up “have I done something wrong?” and answered it explicitly.
Idea (her baby is in danger and she caused it), concern (problems at birth, baby born ill), expectation (to understand and know what happens next).
Fetal movements, pre-eclampsia symptoms and symptomatic hyperglycaemia checked; HbA1c at diagnosis via the team.
Gestational diabetes vs possible pre-existing type 2 diabetes (HbA1c at diagnosis).
Screened reduced fetal movements and pre-eclampsia; knows fasting glucose 7.0 or more means immediate insulin.
Joint clinic within 1 week, self-monitoring targets, diet and activity, metformin then insulin, growth scans, birth planning.
Blame removed; long-term type 2 risk; next-pregnancy testing; follow-up after first clinic.
Reduced movements and pre-eclampsia symptoms to maternity urgently; postnatal FPG at 6–13 weeks; annual HbA1c.

social.t: Weight and diabetes carry stigma; pregnant women often blame themselves. Address it directly and without judgement.
Frequent finger-prick testing, clinic visits and diet change add to pregnancy demands. Ask what support she has, without assuming.

legal.t: Pregnant women and those who have had a baby in the previous 12 months are entitled to free NHS prescriptions with a valid maternity exemption certificate.
Employees are entitled to reasonable paid time off for antenatal appointments, including the joint clinic.

professional.t: The GP’s role is to confirm the joint-clinic referral, support understanding, and record gestational diabetes so the postnatal test and annual HbA1c recall happen.
GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share risk information in a way the patient can understand, balanced and without undue alarm.

community.t: Record the diagnosis for recall; the NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme can support women at high risk of type 2 diabetes if eligible.

redFlags: Severe headache, visual disturbance, pain below the ribs, vomiting or sudden swelling (pre-eclampsia)
Marked thirst, polyuria or feeling unwell (significant hyperglycaemia)
Fasting glucose 7.0 or more at diagnosis (immediate insulin)
psychosocial: Self-blame about weight and family history
Fear for the baby and the birth
ice: Idea: her baby is in danger and she caused it
Concern: something going wrong at birth or the baby born ill
Expectation: to understand the result and what happens next

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “The test shows gestational diabetes: pregnancy hormones are making it harder for your body to control sugar. It usually goes away after the birth.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The placenta makes hormones that act like a brake on insulin. In most women the body presses harder on the accelerator to keep up. In some, it can’t quite, so sugar rises. We help it keep up.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked if your baby is in danger and whether you caused this. You didn’t cause it, and keeping your sugar on target is exactly what protects your baby.”
management.psychosocial: Remove blame; slow the information down; follow-up call after the first clinic; signpost reliable information instead of online searching.
sharedPlan: Joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week (NG3)
Self-monitoring: fasting below 5.3; 1 hour below 7.8 or 2 hours below 6.4 mmol/L
Diet with dietitian support and activity, such as walking after meals
Metformin if targets not met in 1–2 weeks; insulin if still not met
Growth and fluid scans every 4 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks; birth planning, by 40+6 if uncomplicated
Fasting plasma glucose 6–13 weeks after birth; annual HbA1c; early testing next pregnancy
safetyNet: Maternity unit immediately for reduced or changed fetal movements
Maternity unit urgently for headache, visual change, pain below the ribs, vomiting or sudden swelling
Follow-up call after the first joint clinic

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is either frightening her with a list of complications or falsely reassuring her. The marks sit in honest risk anchored on control, removing blame, and a concrete plan she can repeat.

items.fail: Listing complications with no reassuring message.
items.why: She leaves more frightened and less able to engage.
items.fix: Name the main risks, then: “Keeping your sugar on target greatly reduces them.”

items.fail: No mention of the joint clinic or its timing.
items.why: NG3 asks for review in a joint diabetes and antenatal clinic within 1 week.
items.fix: Confirm the referral and the timescale.

items.why: The postnatal fasting glucose at 6–13 weeks and annual HbA1c are commonly missed.
items.fix: “A fasting blood test 6 to 13 weeks after the birth, then every year.”

items.fail: Answering the medical questions but ignoring “Have I done something wrong?”
items.fix: “You haven’t done anything wrong. Pregnancy hormones cause this.”

items.why: Adds guilt and may reduce acceptance later.
items.fix: “Needing metformin or insulin just means the hormones are strong.”

items.fail: No safety-net for fetal movements or pre-eclampsia.
items.fix: Name reduced movements and pre-eclampsia symptoms, and who to call.
